title: What a share is
summary: Ownership, dividends, votes, and why the price moves
body:
A share is a small slice of ownership in a company. If a company were split into a billion equal pieces, one share would be one of those pieces.

Owning one gets you three things. A claim on the profits, often paid out as dividends. A vote at the annual meeting. And a price that rises or falls as investors change their minds about what the company's future profits are worth.

Companies sell shares to raise money. The first time a company does this publicly is an IPO (initial public offering). Anthropic filed for one this week. After that, shares trade between investors on a stock exchange, and the company only sees the money from that first sale.

The price you see is simply the last price two people agreed to trade at. That is why it moves all day.

One UK quirk to learn early: London prices are usually quoted in pence, written p or GBX. SSE at 2,485p is £24.85 a share.
quiz_q: SSE shares closed at 2,485p on Monday. What is one share worth in pounds?
quiz_explain: UK prices are in pence, and 100p is £1, so divide by 100: 2,485p is £24.85.

title: How a stock market works
summary: Exchanges, buyers and sellers, and the bid–ask spread
body:
A stock market is simply a place where people who want to sell shares meet people who want to buy them. Today that place is a computer system run by an exchange, such as the London Stock Exchange or Nasdaq in New York.

The exchange doesn't set prices. It keeps an order book: a live list of everyone offering to sell, and at what price, and everyone wanting to buy, and at what price. When a buyer and a seller agree, a trade happens, and that price becomes the latest share price.

So at any moment there are two prices, not one. The bid is the most anyone is currently willing to pay. The ask (or offer) is the least anyone is willing to sell for. The ask is always a little higher than the bid, and the gap between them is called the spread.

Here's a real example from this morning. The spread is 2p, under 0.1% of the price. If you bought and immediately sold, you would lose that 2p a share before the price had moved at all.

Big, busy shares like SSE, Microsoft or the global tracker funds have tight spreads because huge numbers trade every day. Smaller, quieter shares can have spreads of 1% to 5%, which quietly eats into returns.

Who makes sure there is always someone to trade with? Firms called market makers stand ready to buy and sell all day, and the spread is how they get paid.

Markets also keep hours. London trades from 8:00 to 16:30 UK time and New York from 14:30 to 21:00 UK time. Prices can still move outside those hours: Enphase fell about 16% in after-hours trading last night after its results, so a share can open far from where it closed.

For a long-term investor the lesson is simple. The spread is a hidden cost each time you trade, so trading less, and sticking to busy shares and funds, keeps more of your money working.
quiz_q: SSE is quoted at 2,489p to sell and 2,491p to buy. What is the spread?
quiz_explain: The spread is the gap between the buying and selling prices: 2,491p minus 2,489p is 2p.

title: Indices
summary: What the FTSE 100 and S&P 500 actually measure
body:
An index is a single number that tracks the prices of a basket of shares, so you can see in one glance how a whole market did. The FTSE 100 follows the 100 biggest companies listed in London; the FTSE 250 follows the next 250; the S&P 500 follows 500 large US companies.

The number itself (10,694 for the FTSE 100 last night) has no meaning on its own. What matters is how it changes: a 1% rise in the index means the basket, on average, rose about 1%.

Most big indices use market-cap weighting. A company's market cap is its share price times the number of shares, so giants count for much more than minnows. In the S&P 500, a handful of tech giants like Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia and Alphabet make up a large slice of the index. When they move, the whole index moves.

Wednesday showed why it pays to know which index you're looking at. But the FTSE 250 fell 0.3%, because it holds more UK-focused firms such as housebuilders, which slid 6-7%. Same country, same day, different story.

In the US, the S&P 500 rose 0.3% even though Nvidia fell 1.2%. Because it's weighted by size, the gains elsewhere in big tech outweighed it.

Indices also matter because you can buy one. A tracker fund simply copies an index.

Two things to remember: an index tells you about the average, not about your own shares; and most indices you see quoted ignore dividends, so they slightly understate what investors actually earned.
quiz_q: On Wednesday the FTSE 100 rose 0.1% but the FTSE 250 fell 0.3%. What's the best explanation?
quiz_a: One of the indices was calculated wrongly
quiz_b: They hold different companies: the FTSE 250 has more UK-focused firms like housebuilders, which fell
quiz_c: The FTSE 250 only trades in the afternoon
quiz_d: Indices always move in opposite directions
quiz_explain: Each index tracks its own basket of shares, so on a day when housebuilders slumped and big banks rose, the two could easily go different ways.

title: Funds, ETFs and investment trusts
summary: Buying hundreds of companies in one go
body:
Buying one share means betting on one company. A fund lets you buy a small slice of hundreds or thousands of companies in a single purchase. Your money is pooled with other investors' and the fund holds the shares for all of you.

A tracker fund (or index fund) simply copies an index, like the FTSE 100 or a world index. There is no star manager picking shares, so fees are low. The fee you pay each year is the OCF (ongoing charges figure), often well under 0.3%.

An ETF (exchange-traded fund) is a fund that trades on a stock exchange like a share, so its price moves all day. INRG, a clean-energy fund, is an ETF. It owns about 100 clean-energy companies, including Enphase. When Enphase crashed 16% on Wednesday, INRG fell only 1.5%: losses in one company are softened by the rest. On Thursday Enphase bounced 3.5% and INRG barely moved.

An investment trust is different again. It is a company listed on the stock market whose business is owning other assets. Because a trust has a fixed number of shares, its share price can drift away from the value of what it owns, its NAV (net asset value). When the share price is below NAV, it trades at a discount; above, at a premium. On Thursday Greencoat published its latest NAV, and TRIG finished selling its stake in the Beatrice offshore wind farm. That is the kind of news that can narrow or widen a trust's discount.

Thursday also showed how a broad fund behaves. Alphabet fell nearly 13%, its worst day on record.

The trade-off: a fund spreads your risk, but you also give up the chance that one brilliant pick makes you rich. For most long-term investors that is a good swap.
quiz_q: Why did INRG fall only about 1.5% on the day Enphase, one of its holdings, crashed 16%?
quiz_a: INRG's managers sold Enphase before the fall
quiz_b: Enphase is only one of about 100 companies in the fund, so the others cushioned the drop
quiz_c: ETFs are protected from losses by the stock exchange
quiz_d: INRG is priced in pence, which makes falls smaller
quiz_explain: A fund spreads your money across many companies, so one company's crash moves the whole fund much less.

title: Why diversify
summary: Why one share is riskier than a hundred
body:
Diversification means spreading your money across many different investments so that no single one can do too much damage. The old saying is "don't put all your eggs in one basket", and Friday gave a perfect real-world demonstration.

On Friday Intel, one of the best-known chip companies in the world, fell 28.6% in a single day after giving a disappointing forecast. Anyone with most of their money in Intel lost more than a quarter of it before the weekend. Yet the S&P 500, which contains Intel alongside 499 other companies, fell only 1.8%. Intel is a tiny slice of that index, so its crash was cushioned by everything else.

ASML fell 6.1%, Schneider Electric 4.1% and Nvidia 4.2%. But a broad global fund like Vanguard's ESG Global All Cap dropped 1.9%, because it owns thousands of companies in dozens of countries and industries. Meanwhile AstraZeneca jumped 7%.

There's a catch worth knowing: diversification only works if your investments don't all move together. Owning ten chip companies isn't really ten separate bets, because they tend to rise and fall as a group (investors call this being highly correlated). On Friday nearly every chip stock fell at once. True diversification means mixing different industries, regions and types of investment.

Diversification also has a cost: it caps your upside. If you'd put everything in AstraZeneca, Friday would have been brilliant. But nobody knows in advance which share will be the winner, and research shows most individual shares do worse than the overall market over long periods, while a few big winners do most of the heavy lifting. Owning the whole market makes sure you hold those winners.
quiz_q: On Friday Intel fell 28.6% but the S&P 500 fell only 1.8%. What best explains the difference?
quiz_a: Intel is not part of the S&P 500
quiz_b: The S&P 500 holds 500 companies, so one company's crash is a small part of the total
quiz_c: Index funds are protected from losses
quiz_d: The S&P 500 only contains defensive companies
quiz_explain: Intel is in the S&P 500, but as one small slice among 500 companies its 29% fall barely dented the whole index.
